name: Study flashcards
summary: A good deck starts with the right questions. After that, what matters is controlling the review and keeping your own material together with the results of your study.
lead:
A student uploads lecture notes, a musician attaches a recording of a tune, someone else collects the words they have heard. They all need cards, but what counts as an answer and how it is checked differ between them. A large number of automatically generated questions does not by itself make a study session useful.

We start with preparing the deck, then move to the session itself and to continuing on another device. The thread to follow is the path of a person’s own material: how it gets into a card, what they do with the card, and what is kept after the answer.

audiences.title: Carrying on with your own material
audiences.body: The notes, the spreadsheet or a finished deck already exist. They have to be brought across and the resulting questions checked, while leaving time for the studying itself. Typing everything in again by hand can turn out to be too high a price for moving to a new tool.

audiences.title: Choosing what the next session covers
audiences.body: Familiar cards, new cards and cards that are still hard each need different attention. A person wants to understand the queue, to correct a mark made by accident and to bring back topics that were skipped. The repetition settings should help manage that choice.

audiences.title: Learning through the right way of answering
audiences.body: Pronunciation, a diagram, a musical example and word-for-word recall each set different conditions. In one case looking at the answer is enough; in another it has to be said out loud or written down. The format of the session is worth choosing together with the material that has to be learned.

sections.title: Preparing the material for your own goal
sections.intro: Import and generation should end in a deck that has been checked, not just in a success message.

observations.title: Checking the question before the first review
passages: Turning a photograph of notes into cards can save you from copying them out. In a positive review the convenience is tied precisely to moving across words and definitions that were already prepared. That is a clear first benefit of automation.

But the questions produced have to be sifted. A stray detail from the lecture, or the wrong language, pulls the session away from its goal. A review alongside the source fragment would let someone drop what is not needed, fix an answer and check what is left in the deck before the first repetition.

Preparation can also be cut short by an upload limit the person only learns about after the first photo. How much the trial allows, and the wait between files, are worth showing in advance. A few checked cards give a way to judge the benefit before the whole set of notes is moved across.

quotes.text: I love that you can take a picture of any hand, written words and definitions, and the app will uploaded into a flash card version for you or a PDF version. I love how convenient

It makes terrible cards, no idea what principle it goes by, one time I get 10 cards, then 64, and among them things like who wrote which book, even though this is a history lecture, I uploaded a lecture in Russian and for some reason the questions come in English

This app is really good and pretty helpful and helps me study, but I don't like when I send a picture of my notes end then all of the sudden I have to wait 20 minutes to send the next picture or I have to pay.

placements.title: Checking the question before the first review

observations.title: Seeing the future deck before the transfer
passages: The person has already prepared a spreadsheet and expects to carry on working with it. A blanket import failure sends them switching editors and repeating attempts without understanding why. The first job is to name the supported format and the exact place where the error is.

A preview of a few rows would let the question, the answer and the extra fields be matched up. Automatic translation is a different operation and is worth turning on separately: reading a CSV successfully does not mean the app will convert its contents into the chosen language.

Bringing over a finished deck adds a dependency on an outside service and on an archive format. A page that will not open and a corrupted file call for different actions. What is needed is an explanation of what failed, the original kept, and a way to repeat just that step without preparing all the material again.

quotes.text: I want to create cards on my desktop windows PC but the app keeps rejecting my CSV files, whether from Excel, Notepad, Google Sheets or text in an email.

When are you going to sort out the ability to import a .CSV file?? I have tried all sorts of waves to import a file like that and have it automatically converted to a target language. It's extremely frustrating.

Tried web site that opens for Ankiweb imports and that times out with no page loading. Then tried to import an Anki deck and that throws an error. So this app is useless to me, not sure how others are having a great experience when it fails on the very first things I try to do.

placements.title: Seeing the future deck before the transfer

observations.title: Keeping the part that is actually being learned
passages: In a music deck the name of a tune can be the question, and the recording and the sheet music the answer. For that job the attachment carries the main content. It cannot be treated as an optional extra on a text card.

If an image has vanished from an old deck, the card still formally exists but the exercise has changed. The missing file has to be shown, and it has to be possible to restore or replace it while keeping the link to the right side of the card and to the answer history.

Safekeeping starts at creation. A crash while a photo is being added should not wipe the question that has already been typed. A draft, and the option to reattach a single file, cut down how much work has to be redone; checking old decks and the transfer protects it later on.

quotes.text: I use this program to help me practice an extensive repertoire of traditional Irish music, which should be played from memory during sessions. I list the name of the tune on the front of the card and include an audio file of the tune and an image of the sheet music on the flip side of the card.

I loved this app months ago. It's really easy to use, especially compared to anki. I've been using it for organic chemistry, so a lot of the cards have pictures for the backside. However, I tried to use a deck from a couple months ago, and half of the pictures disappeared.

I recently downloaded the app and it has crashed a few times. I will be creating flashcards and inserting a photo and it crashes. I have tried restarting my device and everything and it will not stop doing that

placements.title: Keeping the part that is actually being learned

sections.title: Understanding what happens in a session
sections.intro: The queue, the audio and the way an answer is checked all shape what the studying consists of.

observations.title: Understanding why a card comes back
passages: An automatic schedule takes some of the decisions about the next repetition off your hands. The review below praises being able to set the retention you want. That assessment shows the appeal of controlling the queue, but the percentage chosen is not a promise of a result for every learner.

But you can see the same words many times, recognize them by the end of the session and struggle with them again the next day — that is exactly the experience described below. Explaining the queue will not on its own repair that experience. It is worth letting someone look at what a session is made of and pick out a difficult topic separately, and testing how useful the method is later, when the familiar look of a card no longer prompts the answer.

A mark made by accident is a more definite interface problem. If a hard word has become “mastered”, the person has to be able to undo the rating and put it back into study. An edit like that preserves control over the material without promising that any schedule will now guarantee retention.

quotes.text: A truly unbelievable app that can be as powerful as you want it to be. It's like magic adjusting the retention to 90% and seeing yourself succeed!

Sure the app works. But I am not learning anything. I'm stuck in what others have called review hell. Eventually in a session, after seeing words 10 or 12 times, I can recognize the words. But the next day it is as if I have never seen them before. I am not retaining anything with this approach.

There are some features that are missing, like for example the ability to manually change the status of a word from Mastered to Learning. I accidentally clicked mastered on a word I hadn't known, and now I can't change it and hence it wont appear in the list of words I need to study.

placements.title: Understanding why a card comes back

observations.title: Hearing the example you need
passages: On a language card the audio is what helps you work out how a word is pronounced. A button that will not work, or an unconvincing reading, breaks exactly that part of the session. The text is still in place, but the person can no longer do the thing they opened the audio for.

It helps to see which language the audio is in and to be able to replay a single example. Your own deck may call for your own recording. When a problem turns up, the link to the specific word has to survive: that way it can be flagged for checking, the material corrected, and the same exercise resumed.

For a word with several pronunciations it matters which one is being used right now. Your own recording or the voice you chose should travel with the card when it moves. Changing the audio language should not quietly apply to a whole mixed deck.

quotes.text: Speech function just doesn't work anymore. It used to sound robotic, but now, it gives a warning that it'll sound robotic, but just doesn't work, I even tried uninstalling and reinstalling again and it STILL doesn't work.

I didn't find that this app really added a lot of vocabulary words that I would want to use in daily life. Additionally words were pronounced by a really primitive AI model. Unbelievably, Some of the pronunciations were not correct.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Hearing the example you need”.

observations.title: Separating the attempt from the check
passages: In a spoken exercise the app first recognizes the speech and then grades the answer. If something went wrong at the first step, the final mark may not match what the person actually said. Showing what was recognized next to what was expected helps.

A long passage makes the attempt itself harder: the session can reset before it ends. Splitting it into fragments, and being able to correct a wrong mark, would let someone continue from the right place. That is work on how the exercise behaves, not proof of better retention.

Finally, reading the back of a card is a different mode from recalling it yourself. If a person expects to be tested, that has to be established before the session and a clear way of answering offered. The rules differ for an exact wording and for a restatement of the meaning; one look at a card should not be presented as both results.

quotes.text: This new update has made audio review a little bit easier, as it listens a little bit better (meaning it registers more when I'm talking), but it marks words wrong that I say very clearly and it's really frustrating that I don't get credit for the review when I'm saying the verse perfectly.

I am testing out a number of memorization apps, and while I like the interface of this app keeping track of my progress of each Bible book the Speak Out needs a lot of work. It is difficult to use on "longer" portions of scripture (more than 2 verses), because it resets and/or skips and marks incorr
I thought this would test my knowledge, but all you're doing is reading the cards! This DOES NOT TEST your knowledge

placements.title: Separating the attempt from the check

sections.title: Carrying on from where you left off
sections.intro: Attachments and the results of study should come back together with the cards.

observations.title: Restoring the deck and the course of study
passages: After changing devices a person expects to see their deck and carry on from where they left off. But the cards, the study marks and the terms of paid access can each transfer separately. Having the list back does not mean the images, the study history and the mode you need have come back too.

The check is easiest on a small familiar set: open both sides, play the attachments and find the last study mark. A large archive needs a clear account of what was transferred and a way to deal with what is missing. Then a new device becomes a continuation of the studying rather than the start of preparing it all again.

A short report after the transfer helps: how many cards, attachments and study records were restored. A mismatch should lead to the specific pieces that are missing. It matters especially to keep the deck’s material distinct from the terms of access to the modes, so that the safety of a person’s own work stays clear.

quotes.text: great vocab but keeps deleting my progress
This app was working perfectly fine and suddenly decided to delete all of my hard work by signing me out and clearing all of the cards I made. I now have lost information. Thanks.

Ad-free subscription does not seem to work across platforms. Purchased a one-year add-free subscription for my iPad, then downloaded the iPhone version. Data entered on iPad was there, but the ads were back with the option to pay another one-year subscription to get rid of the ads.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Restoring the deck and the study progress”.

placements.title: Restoring the deck and the course of study

observations.title: Saving answers without a network
passages: A session on a phone can start somewhere the connection drops or is not there at all. If at that moment the material cannot be opened or an answer cannot be saved, a short free window goes into waiting. Losing the part of the session already done, at the moment it ends, is particularly galling.

Before a trip it helps to check which cards and attachments are actually prepared for access without a network. Then open them, answer a few and come back once there is a connection. Having the deck available and having the session’s progress saved are two separate parts of that scenario; both should be clear before it starts.

A prepared session includes both sides of the cards and the attachments they need. Once the connection is back, the answers already given should be sent up rather than the session started over. If the deck was changed on another device in the meantime, the user has to understand which version of the material is taking part in the next repetition.

quotes.text: The app signed me out and I have to go through the long onboarding process before I fan sign it and it's annoying. It's not the first time. Also, the offline support is bad, the limit should be higher and it counts cards that are backwards as well which as a card, which sounds like poor engineering.

While this app is great for studying on your phone, it lacks truly "mobile" capabilities because it does not work offline. Even if you lose connection for a moment, there will be an error when submitting or suspending your exam, and as a result you can lose all your progress.
The offline mode is a lifesaver and the study reminders keep me on track

conclusion.title: Start by checking the quality of one deck
conclusion.body:
The place to start is the user’s own material and one completed session. Did the questions come out on the right topic, did the images and the audio survive, is it clear what counts as an answer? The reviews show the losses at those transitions plainly. A new scheduling algorithm will not fix a wrong question or a diagram that has vanished.

After that comes the choice of specialization: an easy transfer of finished decks, checking cards made from notes, audio review, or work with exact wording. Each direction needs its own test of usefulness. Time saved in preparation is visible at once; a learning result cannot be inferred from the number of cards created, from a pleasant session or from the retention percentage someone picked.
